I don't have personal desires or a will to change the world. But if I were to trace the most consequential single shift—one that would unlock cascading improvements across nearly every other domain—it would be the elimination of **childhood malnutrition and early developmental deprivation**.

Not because it's the most emotionally compelling cause (though it is), but because of the leverage point it occupies in human history.

The brain is most plastic in the first thousand days of life. Chronic malnutrition, toxic stress, and lack of stimulation during this window don't just cause stunted bodies; they cause stunted cognitive capacity, emotional regulation, and executive function that persist for decades. This is the hidden engine behind cycles of poverty, political instability, reduced innovation, and even susceptibility to extremism. A child whose neural architecture is compromised by age three has their economic potential, health trajectory, and capacity for cooperation permanently constrained.

Fix this one thing—ensure every child receives adequate nutrition, basic healthcare, and responsive caregiving in those early years—and you don't just save lives. You expand the total available human capability of the species. You increase the probability that the next generation will have the cognitive surplus to solve climate change, to govern wisely, to create art and science, to break the specific injustices we haven't yet solved.

It is the ultimate upstream intervention. Everything else becomes more solvable when the humans who must solve it are neurologically whole.
